text.p: "If we assigned grades for portfolio diversification, most investors would earn D's," writes analyst Olivia Barbee in the current issue of Morningstar Investor, a mutual fund newsletter.

That's despite the fact that diversification is the one portfolio-boosting technique that has just about all of the pros in agreement. If you just invest in one security -- or one type of security -- you'll have a heck of a roller coaster ride (if you're lucky enough not to have a free fall) but you won't come out ahead of a carefully mixed portfolio.
A diversified portfolio has a synergistic effect: Designed correctly, it can deliver most of the bang of the riskier securities, with much less of the volatility.
The problem is that it can be confusing to create that careful mix, and many people do it the wrong way.
Take international stocks. If you've taken in any investment advice in the last five years, you've probably been told that international stocks are a good way to balance U.S. stocks.

So what have many people done about that? They've bought so-called "global" or "worldwide" stock funds. And what have the managers of those funds done? Loaded up on boomtime U.S. stocks! So much for diversification.

If you want a properly diversified portfolio, the easiest way to do it is this: Figure out how you want your assets allocated among broad groups, such as large company stocks, small company stocks and bonds, U.S. stocks and bonds and foreign securities. Then, find funds that specialise as narrowly as possible in those selected areas.
For example, instead of a global or worldwide fund, buy an international stock fund. They cannot invest in U.S. stocks, but only those issued in foreign countries.

When diversifying your portfolio, there are a few other points to remember, too: Look for funds that do invest the bulk of their money in the assets and styles in which they specialise: An international stock fund that has 30 percent of its money sitting in ready cash won't give you the same mix as one that's 100 percent invested in international stocks.

In an overheated summer like this, it's also important to keep rebalancing your portfolio. You might have started 1997 with 50 percent of your portfolio in American stocks and another 15 percent in foreign stocks; given the U.S. runaway market and the dismal performance of the Japanese market, among others, you're likely to have much more in U.S. stocks and less in foreign stocks.
The fix? Go back to 50/15. You'll be buying Japan cheap and selling America high.

The time to do that is now, or on a regular schedule of every six months or so, and not once you get the idea that the U.S. market is at a top and the Japanese market -- to repeat the same example -- at a bottom.
And that brings us to the last bit of diversification advice: The key to long-term investment success through diversification is to plan a mix and stick to it through regular rebalancing.
If you find yourself continually trying to time the market just right, or picking up the latest best performing fund, or jumping on any bandwagon whatsoever, you probably aren't properly diversified.
